articles.title: Wales beat New Zealand for first time since 1953
articles.excerpt: Wales edged New Zealand 35-28 in the Nations Championship in Cardiff on Saturday to claim their first victory over the…
articles.fullText:
Wales edged New Zealand 35-28 in the Nations Championship in Cardiff on Saturday to claim their first victory over the All Blacks since 1953.

Scrum-half Tomos Williams scored one of five Welsh tries in a superb individual performance as the home side ended a 34-match losing run against the three-time Rugby World Cup winners.

Wales's heroic defence held out the visitors in the final 25 minutes after the All Blacks had made it a seven-point game thanks to Peter Lakai's try.

The victory is even more remarkable with Welsh rugby in dire straights after a poor run of results since the 2023 World Cup, and a long line of off-field issues overshadowing the sport in the country.

Meanwhile, Will Joseph marked his first Test start with a record-equalling five tries as England thrashed Japan 78-15 in their Nations Championship clash at Twickenham on Sunday.

The recalled Gloucester wing, winning just his second cap, seized his chance to stake a claim for a place in England coach Steve Borthwick's squad for next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia in style.

The younger brother of former England international Jonathan Joseph, Will struck as early as the opening minute.

England crossed Japan's line eight times in a first half that finished with Borthwick's men out of sight at 49-10 and Joseph having run in four of England's eventual 13 tries.

An utterly lopsided encounter saw England post both their highest score and record-winning margin against Japan, surpassing a 60-7 success at the 1987 Rugby World Cup in Australia.

Joseph had a hat-trick inside an opening quarter when England scored five tries as they capitalised on a man advantage after Japan lock Harry Hockings was given a 20-minute red card for a high tackle on Ellis Genge.

And when Joseph went over in the 57th minute off an intercept, he became just the fifth player to score five tries in a Test for England after Douglas Lambert, Rory Underwood, Josh Lewsey and Henry Arundell.

Earlier, Argentina survived late nerves to beat winless Italy 19-14 in a scrappy Nations Championship in Genoa on Saturday.

Italy had lost all four of their games in the first year of the inter-hemisphere tournament without even collecting a bonus point but took a fourth minute lead.

The result left Italy doomed to finish last in the Northern Hemisphere pool.

They face Fiji in their last match in Udine on November 21 and could face the same opponent again the following weekend in the wooden-spoon match at the finals at Twickenham.

Argentina, whose only previous win in the competition was at home to Wales in July, overtook Australia to climb to third in the Southern Hemisphere pool.

They face Northern leaders France next weekend in Paris. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Exclusive: Internal ledgers show how Pyongyang steals wages from its workers in China
articles.excerpt: Paper trail obtained by RFA confirms to the outside world that Pyongyang takes a cut of about 90%.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean

[Editor's Note] Radio Free Asia recently obtained internal documents, on-site videos, and photos from a North Korean overseas dispatch company that has sent laborers to China. Most of these materials were produced in the first half of 2025 and include contracts between North Korean and Chinese companies as well as details on the “application of employee living expenses,” which is how their wages are classified. RFA has also secured a significant number of videos and photos of North Korean workers employed at Chinese companies. RFA’s analysis of these materials presents a harsh reality for these workers that includes stolen pay and poor working conditions. To protect sources, some parts of the documents will be redacted, and only selected scenes from the videos will be released as still images.

The North Korean government confiscates around 90% of the wages earned by workers it dispatches to China, internal documents obtained by Radio Free Asia revealed.
Sources in China have previously told RFA that the North Korean companies that handle the dispatched workers in China collect their wages and forward most of the money to Pyongyang in the form of “ loyalty funds ,” extra support for state projects, and other fees.
According to the sources, a Chinese company will typically pay around 2,500 to 4,000 yuan (about US$375 to $600) per month for every North Korean dispatched worker, but the worker will actually only receive 100 to 300 yuan ($15 to $45).
But the documents – which were made in early 2025 – include contracts, ledgers and other accounting records and are the first known instance where the deductions for the state are confirmed in print.
One contract, between a clothing company in China’s Liaoning province and a North Korean worker dispatch agency shows the details regarding the workers’ wages:
A contract signed in May 2025 between a clothing company in China's Liaoning Province and a North Korean overseas dispatch agency.
(Kim Jieun/RFA) According to Article 4, Clause 1 of the contract, the Chinese company will pay the dispatch company a monthly rate of 5,000 yuan for managers; 4,000 yuan for “assistants” – actually a worker surveillance agent dispatched by Pyongyang’s State Security Ministry; and 4,000 yuan for interpreters. The Chinese company will pay 3,500 yuan for “skilled workers” – the majority of the dispatched personnel, and this includes meal expenses. Clause 2 states that during a two-month training period, the Chinese company will pay 1,500 yuan per North Korean worker.
According to a contract signed in May 2025 between a clothing company in China's Liaoning Province and a North Korean overseas dispatch agency, the wage for non-management-level workers was set at 3,500 yuan.
(Kim Jieun/RFA) On paper, it appears that each North Korean worker could expect to be paid a wage of 3,500 yuan (about $525) per month. This would be a hefty sum, enough to buy close to a metric ton (2,200 pounds) of rice in a North Korean marketplace, at a time when most domestic North Korean workers can’t even afford a single kilogram with their monthly salaries.
But an examination of other documents shows a discrepancy between what the contract stipulates and what the manager of the dispatched workers recorded. The dispatched companies classify the workers’ wages as “living expenses.” A “Living Expense Analysis Table,” that the manager sent to the North Korean headquarters shows that the company received only 2,600 yuan per worker per month. The discrepancy is not accounted for in the documents.
It is highly likely that the manager in this case was setting aside slush funds with the approval of the headquarters’ president, Ri Jong Ho, a former high-ranking official at an organization under Office 39 , the clandestine group formed in the 1970s to manage slush funds for the North Korean leadership, told RFA.
“The president of the headquarters in Pyongyang must provide imported goods and foreign currency demanded daily by officials of powerful institutions,” he said. “It is highly probable that he asks the dispatched manager for help each time.”
Ri explained that the manager has to come up with the money somehow and the only way to do this is to dip into the wages.
“Discrepancies between the contracted amount and the reported amount are a phenomenon that frequently occurs,” he said.
The living expenses table shows that the remaining 2,600 yuan is further reduced before the workers get their share: 1,000 for “state contributions,” 300 for “food expenses,” 500 for “maintenance costs” for the managers’ Chinese office, and 300 for “management expenses” for the Pyongyang headquarters.
A table of expenses reported to the headquarters in Pyongyangin early 2025 by a North Korean official dispatched to a clothing company in Liaoning Province, China.
(Kim Jieun/RFA) After calculating these items, the North Korean official reported to headquarters that living expenses per employee were paid at an average of 800 yuan, a maximum of 1,100 yuan, and a minimum of 450 yuan. However, after each itemized deduction, the remaining amount for the workers is only 500 yuan, less than the reported average wage of 800 yuan. It is therefore highly likely that the actual wages paid to workers are lower than the listed “average amount” and closer to the “minimum amount.”
If the average pay is the remaining 500 yuan, that represents an 86% total deduction from the contracted wage.
Reported wages vs. reality
Similar wage deductions were observed in communications between managers of North Korean workers and the Pyongyang headquarters. According to another contract obtained by RFA between a food company in Liaoning and a North Korean dispatching company, the wage for a skilled worker is 4,000 yuan, slightly higher than the 3,500 yuan paid by the clothing company.
However, the dispatching company reported that it received 2,200 yuan per worker. Just as before, the discrepancy is not accounted for in any documentation. From the base of 2,200 yuan, 1,000 was deducted for “state contribution,” and 300 for food expenses, leaving 900 for the workers. The average pay was listed at a maximum of 900 yuan and a minimum of 500.
A table of expenses reported to the Pyongyang headquarters in early 2025 by a North Korean official dispatched to a food company in Liaoning Province.
(Kim Jieun/RFA) The Multinational Sanctions Monitoring Team, or MSMT, an intergovernmental organization that helps U.N. member states enforce sanctions on North Korea, estimated the number of North Korean workers in China to be between 20,000 and 70,000 in a report published Sept. 16.
Assuming that each worker pays a state contribution of roughly 1,000 yuan, the amount collected by the North Korean authorities reaches between 20 million and 70 million yuan ($3 million to $10.5 million).
Even considering the paltry remnants of their salary that they should be receiving, that can be reduced even further when the government requires donations or subsidies for state projects. The expense ledger submitted by a North Korean manager dispatched to a Chinese clothing company which covered the six years between 2019 and 2025, detailed these mandatory donations.
According to the ledger, donations and grants are broadly divided into three types. The first is the “Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il Fund,” named after the North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s father and grandfather, who are also his predecessors. The fund is nominally for the upkeep of the Kumsusan Palace of the Sun in Pyongyang – a mausoleum where the former leaders are enshrined – and other projects related to commemorating their lives.
The amount of donations to this fund varied over the years, starting with the workers donating a collective 3,000 yuan in 2019, climbing to 11,500 in 2020, then dropping into the 3,000 to 10,000 range until hitting 16,000 in 2024. The ledger showed that in the first four months of 2025, they had already donated 16,000 yuan.
The second listed type of deduction is funding for idolization projects. The manager reported to headquarters the amount paid as support for “proceeding with the work to forever hold the Great Marshals in high esteem as the Sun of Juche,” with the sun referring to the poetic representation of national founder Kim Il Sung, who created the country’s founding Juche ideology of self-reliance.
According to the document, in 2019, the company as a whole donated 3,000 yuan to the North Korean consulate’s flower exhibition featuring the Kimjongilia, a begonia named after the late former leader on the occasion of his 46th birthday in 1988, prior to his ascension following the death of his father in 1994.
The workers also donated in 2024 a combined US$7,000 for the Samjiyon Project , Kim Jong Un’s ambitious plan to construct a modern socialist paradise at the foot of Mount Paektu, the tallest mountain in Korea and the setting of many of the ancient founding myths of the Korean people, and the modern myths related to the birth of Kim Jong Il.
The company also donated 5,000 yuan for upkeep at the Sino-Korean Friendship Exhibition, a museum in North Korea dedicated to friendly relations with China.
The third and final item on the ledger is for operating expenses at the North Korean consulate and support funds for the fatherland spent under the pretext of “patriotic activity projects.” Collectively 200,000 to 300,000 yuan was donated annually for these. In particular, in 2023 and 2024, 20,000 yuan each was spent on “military industry support” projects under the consulate support category.
“Cash is provided to the Ministry of Military Industry to purchase materials necessary for the modernization of military factories,” Ri said. “This is in accordance with Kim Jong Un’s orders and directives.”
Fatherland support projects
Between 150,000 and 260,000 yuan were collectively donated annually on projects supporting the fatherland, accounting for the largest share among the donation categories.
Specifically, 50,000 yuan was contributed in July 2020 for the construction of the Pyongyang General Hospital , 170,000 yuan in 2021 for COVID-19 prevention , 50,000 yuan in 2024 for agriculture and housing improvement, and 60,000 yuan for flood damage recovery .
This demonstrates that the costs of the new national tasks and policy projects proposed by the North Korean authorities are being significantly covered by the wages of workers employed by overseas dispatch companies.
Details of the 2024 Consulate and Fatherland support projects reported to Pyongyang headquarters by a North Korean company manager dispatched to a Chinese clothing manufacturer.
(Kim Jieun/RFA) Looking at the year 2024 alone, the total amount spent by this company under various pretexts reached 352,000 yuan ($52,000). This strongly implies that workers’ wages are used as a source of funding for the company’s various contributions and support projects.
Sources in China told RFA that managers of dispatched workers are evaluated based on how much they can contribute to fatherland improvement funds, so there are incentives to force the workers to donate from the tiny amounts they are paid.
“They make one or two people contribute large amounts of funds or subsidies, citing them as models of loyalty to compel other workers to follow suit, or assign workers who pay more to work easier jobs,” a source in China who requested anonymity for security reasons, told RFA.
Official kickbacks and various donations are not the only channels through which wages are siphoned off. Managers and executives also embezzle funds, sources said. This is done by making deductions for cosmetics, clothing, toilet paper and food at a significant markup.
Dispatch agencies restrict external access out of fear that the workers might escape, leaving them with no choice but to request and purchase necessary supplies from the company, forcing them to pay whatever price the manager sets for these.
The reason North Korean workers’ wages can be reduced so easily appears to be due to the method of storing cash in safes.
“Living expenses are collected in individual envelopes for each person and stored in a safe in the office,” a manager at a North Korean dispatch company in China reported to the Pyongyang headquarters.
According to sources, workers merely record their monthly living expenses and costs for daily necessities in the company ledger. They do not handle the cash directly. Wages are settled and received all at once upon their return home. Since the cash is kept in a company safe inaccessible to the workers, the amount they receive depends on the company’s ledger, which the managers can edit at any moment.
Ultimately, after all the various deductions and forced donations, the actual amount received by each worker is around 100 to 300 yuan ($15 to $45) per month. The source told RFA that there are many workers who did not even receive 10,000 yuan ($1,500) when they returned home, despite having worked in China for nearly 10 years.
Fraction of wages paid out upon return
Although their nominal salaries are many times what they could be earning in government-assigned jobs back home, MSMT’s report explained that the North Korean dispatched workers often return home with debt.
“The DPRK government confiscates 80-90% of wages earned by North Korean labourers. In some cases, the confiscated amount exceeds their actual earnings, leaving North Korean overseas labourers indebted to the DPRK government.”
Due to the anxiety that they might not receive proper wage settlements upon returning home, some workers prepare for this “wage disappearance” by buying up daily necessities from China and reselling them in North Korea. One worker even declared “20 bags weighing 50 kilograms each” as the luggage he was to take back.
Due to anxiety that they will not receive their full wages during the settlement process upon returning home, some workers prepare for this "wage disappearance" by buying up daily necessities from China through supervisors or officials and reselling them in North Korea. This document shows the contents of 20 separate bags packed by a single returning North Korean worker. The items include food, shoes, specific articles of clothing and even coffee and toothpaste.
(Kim Jieun/RFA) “The Multinational Sanctions Monitoring Team report identified the Workers’ Party’s Office 39 and others as organizations involved in the dispatch of overseas workers,” said Ri. “Workers whose contracts state a salary of 3,500 yuan actually receive a maximum of 300 yuan, while the rest goes to Pyongyang under the names of state contributions and various donations to make up Kim Jong Un’s slush funds.”
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Filipino fishermen urge Manila to defend territorial waters – their fishing grounds
articles.excerpt: Philippines will look to finalize South China Sea code of conduct during ASEAN meetings in Manila next week.
articles.fullText:
MANILA, Philippines - Ahead of two major international meetings for Manila next week, fishermen in the Philippines are urging their government to press the international community on territorial disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea that they say are responsible for a decreased catch, the fishermen told Radio Free Asia.
The Philippines will host a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, from Nov. 15 to 17. In addition to the 10 leaders of the regional economic bloc, leaders of other global partners are also attending, including U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese Premier Li Qiang.
Immediately after the ASEAN Summit, many of the same leaders will fly to Shenzhen, China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, leaders meetings.
The meetings come at a crucial time for the Philippines, as analysts say Manila will try to rally the international community to their side in disputes over waters in the South China Sea that are claimed both by the Philippines and China. Manila hopes to finalize a “code of conduct” governing actions in the sea region at the ASEAN summit, but analysts and observers are doubtful that the agreement will be completely hammered out before it ends.
China’s incursions into the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone are directly to blame for dwindling fish catches, Joey Marabe, a Filipino fisherman, told RFA.
“We used to fish in Scarborough Shoal with other fishermen from other nations,” he said. But when China began claiming it as their own, “we were accused of stealing resources and fish in our own seas.”
Rising Tension
Scarborough Shoal is a rich fishing ground within the EEZ of the Philippines, but has been under Chinese control since 2012. Marabe hails from the coastal town of Masinloc, about 150 kilometers (94 miles) northwest of Manila. The shoal lies due west.
China claims territory within its “nine-dash line,” which essentially encircles the entirety of the South China Sea, including the shoal.
After escalating tensions that ultimately led to a standoff over the shoal in 2012, Manila took the dispute to the international arbitration court. The court issued a ruling in 2016 that invalidated the nine-dash line, but Beijing rejects the ruling and still maintains control of the shoal.
Marabe, a leader in the fishermen’s rights group Pamalakaya, said that a code of conduct for the South China Sea between China and ASEAN must put the welfare of fishermen first, and the regional bloc must be willing to work together to ensure that China follows through on its commitments.
“The government must also be prepared to fight and defend our sovereign rights,” he said.
Filipinos need to put their domestic political differences aside and speak to China with a singular voice to get a code of conduct done, Rodrigo Laudit, a fisherman from the coastal community of Las Piñas in Manila, told RFA. He said fishermen would be the most affected by the code, or lack thereof.
The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs “should lead all agencies of the government that are dealing with WPS in this,” he said, using the abbreviation of the West Philippine Sea, the part of the South China Sea inside the Philippines’ EEZ. “Above the dwindling catch, it is Filipinos’ sovereignty that is at stake here.”
But diplomacy can only go so far, Dindo Manhit, president of the Manila-based Stratbase Institute, told RFA.
“It cannot replace transparency and public accountability,” he said, warning against diplomatic considerations that could potentially weaken defense of sovereignty.
Manhit’s comments are in response to recent debates over how Manila should walk the tightrope of responding to Beijing’s encroachments into its EEZ while also maintaining good relations with China, a major economic partner.
Discretion and diplomacy can work, but they “must never be used to suppress scrutiny or silence officials on matters of core national interests,” he said. “Exposing coercion and unlawful maritime activities is a lawful defense of our rights,” he stressed.
Deescalation?
For now, both sides appear to be dialing down the tension to avoid a further deterioration of diplomacy, recognizing the potential impact of tough talk on bilateral ties and economic discussions, analysts said.
Both sides must also be careful not to undermine their respective diplomatic meetings, Lucio Pitlo, a policy and security analyst based in Manila, told RFA. In October, Beijing sent its lowest-level delegation to a defense ministers’ meeting held in the central Philippine island of Cebu.
Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, center, delivers his opening remarks during the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu, Philippines on Oct. 29, 2026.
(Eloisa Lopez/AFP) “One important goal is to avoid a possible snub or low-level delegation attending each other’s event, which may not look well for the host and affect the enthusiasm of other regional leaders attending the meetings,” he said.
Pitlo, who heads the Philippine Association of Chinese Studies, noted that the foreign ministers of both countries had also recently agreed during a “much-needed phone call to stabilize ties ahead of the back-to-back regional summits.”
During the phone conversation, China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Filipino counterpart Theresa Lazaro that bilateral relations were facing “malicious disruptions” from unnamed Filipino officials who have allegedly smeared China. He called on the Philippines to boost restraint over the officials and send “a rational and unified voice on its policy toward China.”
“For the Philippines, avoiding the economic fall-out from heated verbal and social media exchanges between some Philippine security officials and the Chinese embassy” means that “President Marcos has had to encourage officials to be more cautious about their language, recognizing its potential diplomatic impact,” said Pitlo.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Exclusive: US-sanctioned Jinan Supercomputing Center still gets Nvidia AI products
articles.excerpt: Despite export control restrictions, Chinese research facilities continue acquiring advanced chips.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Mandarin
As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Thursday announced his resignation amidst a scandal over an alleged extramarital affair that may have been a Chinese spy plot targeting him, a Radio Free Asia investigation revealed that sanctioned entities in China were able to get ahold of the company’s AI chips despite U.S. restrictions.
The U.S. government will continue to investigate Jensen Huang’s involvement with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore cloud data center company Megaspeed, who is suspected of collecting intelligence for Beijing and assisting Chinese clients in obtaining restricted chips.
This “AI industry earthquake” triggered by news of Huang’s departure has attracted intense outside attention. After the U.S. restricted direct exports of certain Nvidia products to China starting in 2022 , can sanctioned Chinese institutions still obtain Nvidia computing equipment through overseas cloud services or domestic suppliers?
RFA’s investigation of Chinese government procurement data revealed that Nvidia’s RTX 5090 graphics cards and DGX Spark products appeared in a winning bid announcement for an AI equipment procurement project this year by China’s Shandong Computing Center, also known as the National Supercomputing Center Jinan.
However, according to U.S. government regulations, even if the aforementioned products can enter China, they cannot be purchased or used by the Jinan Center because it appears on a list of export control entities .
On June 17, 2026, the China Government Procurement Network ( web archive ) published a procurement result announcement. The procured item was the “Edge Intelligent Computing Team AI Workstation and Graphics Card Procurement Project.” The winning bidder was Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd., with a winning bid price of RMB 148,500 (US$22,000). The product list in the procurement document contained two items: “RTX5090” and “DGXSPark”, while the brand column indicated “Yixin,” a brand operated by Qiyuan Jiasu.
Information from China Government Procurement Network shows that the Shandong Computing Center, which is subject to U.S. chip sanctions, was still soliciting bids for Nvidia high-end products as of June 2026.
(Government Procurement Network; RFA graphic) Information from China Government Procurement Network shows that the Shandong Computing Center, which is subject to US chip sanctions, was still soliciting bids for Nvidia high-end products as of June 2026. (Screenshot from China Government Procurement Network; RFA graphic)
“RTX 5090” is a graphics card from Nvidia that uses the Blackwell architecture and is equipped with 32GB GDDR7 memory; DGX Spark is a desktop AI computing system launched by Nvidia equipped with the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip.
The procurement quantity for this tender only indicated “one batch” without explicitly specifying how many RTX 5090 graphics cards or how many DGX Spark units were included in “one batch.”
Different restrictions on selling two products into China
RFA further checked Nvidia product categories and U.S. export control regulations, finding that rules for selling the two products into China’s general market are not the same.
The RTX 5090 graphics card has a standard version and a “special edition” tailored specifically for the Chinese market. The former falls under advanced computing products controlled by the U.S. which cannot be shipped to China without an applicable license. The special versions of the card have model numbers RTX 5090 D and RTX 5090 D v2. However, the Jinan Center’s procurement announcement only listed “RTX 5090,” making it impossible to confirm whether the purchase was for the original version or the China special edition.
The DGX Spark, a desktop AI computer equipped with the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, is listed on Nvidia’s official Chinese website with purchasing channels in China. Therefore, the DGX Spark can indeed be sold in China’s general market.
However, availability in China’s general market does not allow for unrestricted sale to entities like the National Supercomputing Center Jinan.
Purchasing party identified by U.S. in 2021
The Shandong Computing Center was established in 1976 and is affiliated with Qilu University of Technology; the National Supercomputing Center Jinan was established in 2011, and both currently belong to the same institutional framework.
The U.S. Department of Commerce’s entity list explicitly listed “Shandong Computing Center” as an alias for “National Supercomputing Center Jinan.” The center was placed on the list in April 2021, prior to the broad export restrictions on advanced computing chips to China that the U.S. began implementing in 2022.
The U.S. Department of Commerce stated at the time that seven Chinese supercomputing and chip institutions, including Jinan, Shenzhen, Wuxi, and Zhengzhou, had procured U.S.-origin items to support Chinese military units, military modernization, and weapons of mass destruction programs. The U.S. determined that these activities were contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
After being added to the entity list , exporting, re-exporting, or transferring items subject to the U.S. Export Administration Regulations, or EAR, within China to the Jinan Center in principle requires a license from the U.S. Department of Commerce, and without a license, it is subject to a presumption of denial. These restrictions target specific transaction counterparties and are not limited to prohibiting high-end AI chips purchased by general Chinese customers.
Chris Tseng, an overseas researcher at Taiwan’s Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology, told RFA that items regulated under the U.S. Export Administration Regulations theoretically require review by the Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS under the U.S. Department of Commerce whenever shipped to an entity on the entity list, even for items with looser control standards.
Tseng added that U.S. export controls travel with the item itself, so even if these two products were shipped to legitimate Chinese or third-country distributors, a license is still required to transfer them to a controlled entity like the Shandong Computing Center.
“The broader issue is that current controls still rely heavily on corporate self-compliance,” he said. “Whether it’s Nvidia tracking customers and end-users, or Chinese and other potential third-country distributors failing to comply with U.S. export rules upon transfer,” both present challenges.
Bloomberg News reported that in inventory verification reports submitted by Nvidia to the U.S. government, it was revealed that approximately 50,000 AI chips sold to Megaspeed were underreported. The uncounted chips were valued at billions of dollars, raising concerns that chips leaked illicitly into China via Southeast Asia.
Ties between the winning supplier and sanctioned distributor
The winning bidder in the deal in RFA’s investigation, Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd., shares multiple noteworthy similarities with Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology, a Chinese company that was once a major Nvidia partner and was later sanctioned by the U.S.
Radio Free Asia reviewed public data for both companies and found that they both describe themselves on their webpages as “a leading artificial intelligence infrastructure solution provider,” using identical text.
The homepages of Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology, top, and Qiyuan Jiasu use the same phrase “a leading artificial intelligence infrastructure solution provider" (in red box).
(Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology, Qiyuan Jiasu; RFA graphic) Both companies also set their production bases in Wuqing, Tianjin, and marketing offices in Shangdi, Beijing. The partner clients listed on both companies’ websites are also completely identical, including Tsinghua University, Peking University, Beijing Institute of Technology, as well as the CAS Institute of Computing Technology, Institute of Automation, Institute of Mechanics, Institute of Remote Sensing, and Institute of Information Engineering; even the phrasing and order listed by both companies are identical.
The partner clients of Qiyuan Jiasu, top, and Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology are identical, listed in the same order (red box).
(Qiyuan Jiasu, Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology; RFA graphic) “Their business registration and website introductions are almost identical,” a commentator familiar with China’s AI industry told RFA in an interview, stating that this strongly raises suspicion that Qiyuan Jiasu might be a new entity taking over part of Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology’s business after it was sanctioned by the US. “This is one company operating under two banners; Qiyuan Jiasu may be a new shell used after Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology was placed on the Entity List.”
Public data shows that Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology had been an NPN authorized partner of Nvidia since 2015 and was described as an Nvidia Elite Partner, DGX Series official authorized value-added reseller, and Tesla Series core partner. Reports from the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area government in 2023 also confirmed its status as an Nvidia Elite Partner.
However, the U.S. Department of Commerce placed Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology on the Entity List sanctions on April 11, 2024, citing that the company acquired US-origin items to support Chinese military modernization.
Li Houchen, a Japan-based current affairs and economic columnist, remarked during an interview that if Qiyuan Jiasu indeed inherited Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology’s original operations, Nvidia would need to investigate the sales and ultimate flow of related products. However, current public information can only verify that the company profiles, client lists, and operational locations of the two companies overlap heavily, with no direct evidence yet proving both belong to the same ultimate beneficial ownership system.
Experts: Export controls have exploitable loopholes
Sylvia Chen, an economic security policy analyst at DSET who previously worked in sanctions and export control legal advisory, told RFA that under current U.S. regulations, third-party enterprises can’t first purchase controlled products and then export or transfer them within China to the National Supercomputing Center Jinan. If carrying out such resales, third-party enterprises may likewise bear legal liability for violating export control regulations.
However, Chen pointed out that practical enforcement faces staffing constraints. Currently, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security has only one export control officer stationed in Beijing responsible for end-use and end-user verification; worldwide, there are only 15 such officers.
From a corporate compliance perspective, suppliers including Nvidia have an obligation to conduct “Know Your Customer” (KYC) procedures. Once suspicious “red flags” appear in a transaction, the enterprise should further verify the product’s end-use, end-user, and destination. If relevant doubts remain unresolved and the company proceeds with the transaction, it may be deemed that Nvidia “should have known” that illegal diversion of the product existed, thereby assuming corresponding liability.
Chen noted that current rules do not mandate companies to continuously track chip locations, though such technology already exists. Public reports indicate Nvidia has offered an opt-in tracking software feature to Blackwell chip customers.
Currently, provisions related to the “Chips Security Act” have been incorporated into amendments proposed by the Senate for the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027, or NDAA. The final text of the FY2027 NDAA will still be confirmed whether the relevant clauses of the Chips Security Act will be retained and ultimately passed into law.
Chen believes that even if the bill fails to pass, the next Congress controlled by Democrats may still reintroduce stricter export control measures.
Tseng told RFA that current supervision mainly consists of three levels: pre-shipment investigation of customers and end-users by Nvidia; post-shipment end-use checks by BIS export control officers; and self-directed spot checks by enterprises regarding product destination, or enhancing oversight via location verification tech under discussion in the Chips Security Act. Additionally, in specific cases, inter-country intelligence sharing and law enforcement cooperation can be used to trace product destinations.
China needs dual-use supercomputing technology
The Jinan Municipal Government’s 2019 publication “Opinions on Accelerating the Industrialization Development of Supercomputing” requires the National Supercomputing Center Jinan to lead the establishment of a collaborative innovation alliance, and to “establish and improve a mechanism for mutual access and sharing of military and civilian technology resources,” perform “joint key research on dual-use supercomputing technology,” and promote the industrialization of related technology.
The same policy document also listed medical health, artificial intelligence, new materials, agricultural disaster prevention, and smart manufacturing as supercomputing application fields. This demonstrates that the Jinan Center simultaneously undertakes civilian scientific research, industrial development, and military-civilian dual-use technology missions, though it cannot be assumed based on this that the equipment procured this time will be used directly for military projects.
Government procurement records show that the Jinan Center conducted this procurement through a Chinese domestic supplier. Public information shows that the winning company, Qiyuan Jiasu, deals in GPU servers, Nvidia graphics cards, and high-performance computing equipment, and has supplied servers to Chinese universities and research institutions in the past.
RFA sent an email to Nvidia asking whether it was aware of this procurement, whether the relevant products obtained applicable U.S. export licenses, and whether it will launch an investigation into this case. No response was received prior to press time.
RFA also inquired with Qiyuan Jiasu and the Shandong Computing Center to learn whether this procurement project had received US authorization or involved smuggling issues; no response has been received yet.
Translation reviewed by Ruo Shui, edited by Charlie Dharapak and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: PNG observers call for restraint from China and US over ‘wine bottle’ shell
articles.excerpt: The statements by Beijing and Washington undermine the jurisdiction of PNG authorities, observers said.
articles.fullText:
PORT MORESBY, Papua New Guinea – The U.S. and China should stop trying to push their own narratives and allow the Papua New Guinea Police to handle the case of an allegedly smuggled artillery shell found in a shipping container imported by a Chinese company, a senior communications expert from the Pacific country told Radio Free Asia.
Police last week confirmed that the shell seized on Oct. 29 was indeed a 130-millimeter round, contrary to the Chinese embassy’s claim on social media that it was merely a harmless wine bottle that was shaped like an artillery shell.

The U.S. Embassy disputed the claim on social media, saying that the U.S. military had “engaged” with the PNG Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit, who determined that it was a Chinese-manufactured artillery projectile.
PNG police detained four Chinese men in connection with the incident.
But letting the U.S. or China influence public opinion through their statements undermines the PNG police and the country’s sovereignty, Joseph Ealedona, a former media executive and former president of Port Moresby Soccer Association, told RFA.
“It is a police investigation and only the PNG police will release details,” he said. “We Papua New Guineans do not come to your country and announce matters under police investigation.”

He called for restraint from the embassies of both countries.
“The Chinese and U.S. Embassies must respect our sovereignty and refrain from making public statements,” he said. “The matter is under active police investigation. It must not be used for geopolitical interests. We are friends to U.S. and China so this must be respected.”
‘A 21st century arms race’
The “wine bottle” shell is part of a “superpower arms race,” former diplomat Dominic Sengi wrote in a commentary published in local newspaper The National.
“PNG and the Pacific has become an increasingly important arena of strategic competition where superpowers come courting and subscribing nations in their spheres,” he wrote.

The smaller Pacific Islands, he said, have welcomed both because they feel like they stand to gain something when the larger powers compete.
“Come one, come all, invest in our country. Build our roads, finance our ports, train our police, support our defense forces. Establish diplomatic missions, bring your development programs – friends to all, enemies to none,” he wrote, describing what he called a “pragmatic, almost laissez-faire” approach to international relations.
“Laissez-faire diplomacy however becomes problematic when welcoming everyone means allowing everyone to pursue their strategic interests without sufficient national scrutiny.”
He said that Beijing and Washington’s competing explanations over the incident are themselves “instruments of political engagement.”
“Both countries speak the language of friendship and mutual respect,” he wrote. “Yet PNG must ask whether these declarations are always identical to the interests of our peoples.”
Papua New Guinea’s closing of Taiwan’s trade office in Port Moresby this month was described as puzzling from a diplomatic standpoint, experts told RFA, but it signals a coming expansion of its economic relationship with China.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Teacher certificate bill proposed
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau has proposed amending the law to enhance the teacher registration mechanism by introducing practising certificate requirements, thereby…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau has proposed amending the law to enhance the teacher registration mechanism by introducing practising certificate requirements, thereby upholding the professionalism of the teaching force. The Government will publish the Education (Amendment) Bill 2026 in the Gazette tomorrow and introduce it to the Legislative Council for first and second readings on November 25.

The bureau noted that it has referenced teacher registration systems in various jurisdictions alongside the registration and practising certificate requirements of other Hong Kong professions. It stated that making a practising certificate a prerequisite for teaching, in addition to the existing statutory registration, could elevate public recognition of the sector and raise the social status of teachers.

The bill will establish statutory rules requiring all teachers and principals of publicly funded schools, private schools, international schools and kindergartens to hold both teacher registration and practising certificates. Each practising certificate will remain valid for a maximum of three school years.

To ensure educators keep abreast of the latest global and local educational policies, teachers must meet a mandatory continuing professional development requirement to obtain a practising certificate. This measure aims to align their knowledge and pedagogy with the evolving needs of students and society.

The bureau pointed out that as role models and key figures in nurturing young people, teachers have a profound impact on students through their conduct, values, words and deeds. Amid rapid societal changes, parents and the wider public hold increasingly high expectations for teacher professionalism.

The bureau highlighted that the bill addresses the practical operational needs of schools, encourages educators to keep pace with the times and strengthens staff management to safeguard student well-being. It also establishes safeguards to bar individuals convicted of offences endangering national security from teaching, protecting students while upholding professional integrity and public confidence.

articles.title: North Korean affordability crisis: monthly salary can’t buy even a bag of rice
articles.excerpt: Workers start every month deep in the red as inflation guts official wages and forces reliance on side hustles.
articles.fullText:
[Editor's Note] To protect the safety of sources inside North Korea who could face severe punishment by authorities if identified, the family featured in this article is a composite model based on reporting from exclusive interviews conducted by RFA Korean journalists with two separate households inside North Korea. One household is a couple working at a state-run factory who shared their wages and living expenses with RFA; the other is a family with middle school and primary school children who detailed their household expenditures. All wages, prices, and expenditure details cited in the article are based on facts confirmed in those interviews. Mr. Kim and Ms. Lee are pseudonyms.

Last month’s take-home pay for Mr. Kim – a 45-year old man who works a government-assigned job in a state-run food processing plant in South Pyongan province – was 20,000 won (about 30 US cents). Although his official wage is set at 50,000 won a month, 30,000 won was deducted upfront as “social support” for state construction projects, education funds, and agricultural supply purchases.
Because production levels and management vary widely across industries and state enterprises in North Korea, worker compensation differs significantly. While well-managed, profitable factories pay higher wages, struggling facilities cannot guarantee even baseline monthly compensation.
Mr. Kim was fortunate to receive any pay at all this month – raw materials arrived on time, keeping his factory’s assembly line running. Workers at other plants were not as lucky. They received nothing when supply shortages ground operations to a halt.
Even though he is one of the lucky ones who got paid, a 20,000-won income cannot buy a single kilogram (2.2 pounds) of white rice – currently priced at over 40,000 won per kilogram – or even a kilogram of corn, which costs around 25,000 won.
Based on October price and wage data verified through sources inside North Korea, RFA compiled a monthly budget for a composite four-member household—comprising factory worker Mr. Kim, his wife Ms. Lee, and their two school-aged children—to illustrate the reality of monthly living expenses.
The reported commodity prices were gathered from South and North Pyongan, South and North Hwanghae, and Kangwon provinces.
A simulated November household budget for a fictional family of four in North Korea shows a monthly deficit of about 1.3 million won (about $18), based on October prices in southern North Korea reported by RFA sources.
(RFA Korean) Starting each month ‘in the red’
With two children attending school, the Kim household budget starts in the red every month.
Schools demand children bring “assignment quotas” of waste paper and scrap metal for recycling – it is a mandatory patriotic offering. Collecting the materials takes a lot of time and effort, so most students pay in cash instead – to the tune of around 30,000 won per month. With two kids, that’s 60,000 won, already triple Mr. Kim’s salary.
On top of that, home utilities cost roughly 5,000 won per month. Even though water and electricity can and do cut out at any given moment, they still have to pay the bill.
Thus the Kim family is already 45,000 won in the hole before factoring in the cost of food.
In some factories, 5 to 10 kilograms (about 10-20 pounds) of corn is said to be supplied to working employees once a month, while in North Hamgyong Province, the rice or prepared food items that were previously provided have been completely cut off. Circumstances differ depending on the region, factory, and enterprise, but at any rate, what families are provided through their workplaces is a mere fraction of what they need to eat each month.
According to the daily food recommendations set by North Korean authorities – 750 grams of corn for workers, 550 grams for housewives and 450 grams for students, the monthly food requirement based on three meals per day for the Kims is about 66 kilograms.
1.65 million won corn deficit. Rice? Keep dreaming
How much money does the Kim family need just to scrape by each month?
According to sources, as of October, the price of white rice traded in North and South Pyongan provinces is about 40,000 won per kilogram, and corn is around 25,000 won. In North Hamgyong and Ryanggang provinces, 1 kilogram of white rice has already exceeded 50,000 won.
If the family relied entirely on white rice, their monthly food bill would reach 2.64 million won—equivalent to 52 months of Mr. Kim’s nominal salary of 50,000 won. Rice is therefore a luxury that only the wealthiest North Koreans can afford. Like most North Koreans, the Kims will get by on a diet of mostly corn. A monthly supply costs a total 1.65 million won, which is 33 times Mr. Kim’s nominal monthly income.
Workers at the Ryuwon footwear factory produce various types of Ryuwon-trademarked shoes in Pyongyang, North Korea, Sept. 25, 2020.
(Jon Chol Jin/AP) Jiro Ishimaru, head of the Osaka-based ASIAPRESS media outlet that covers North Korea, explained, “Currently, with a North Korean worker’s salary, rice is out of the question, and they barely live centered around corn.” Asiapress tracks commodity and food prices in various regions through its contacts in North Korea.
“ In the case of working at a state enterprise, it varies by rank and industry, but roughly the monthly pay provided by the state is between 35,000 won and 100,000 won,” he said. “Even if a well-performing state enterprise pays double the salary at 200,000 won, with that money you cannot even buy 5 kilograms of white rice, and there is no such thing as rations. With such wages, people are barely able to live on a diet centered on corn.”
Under these constraints, balanced meals with adequate protein remain an unaffordable luxury. Pork sells for 270,000 won per kilogram—more than 13 times Mr. Kim’s take-home wage – pollack costs 100,000 won per kilogram, and eggs sell for 10,000 won each.
Other important food-related items are also out of reach. Bottled water runs between 5,000 and 10,000 won per liter, and a 10-liter container of imported Russian cooking oil costs 200,000 to 250,000 won. Although prices vary by quality and region, such items remain entirely unattainable on a 20,000-won salary.
Adding basic daily necessities, staple food supplies like condiments, and transportation expenses, the growing deficit is only made worse when unexpected expenses arise.
So the family somehow needs to earn more money to get by.
Side hustles to feed the family
Like most other families, the Kims need side hustles to bridge the gap between Mr. Kim’s income and their monthly living costs. Ms. Lee used to trade goods in the marketplace to earn money, but then the government started cracking down on informal market activity. Now she has turned to day labor, hauling heavy loads or doing manual labor at construction sites. According to sources, the daily wages people earn from this sort of work can be about 100,000 - 200,000 won. In one day of manual labor, she earns double what her husband earns working a full month at the factory.
However, informal work is irregular. Even if Ms. Lee secures 15 days of labor a month and brings in 1.5 million won, her earnings still fall short of covering the 1.65 million won needed just to buy monthly corn supplies.
Ishimaru explained that there are other types of jobs that people can get to bridge the gap.
“Since official salaries alone are not enough, as all our contacts tell us now, assembling products at home—like wigs or eyelashes—serve as side jobs,” said Ishimaru. .
In October 2023, when North Korean authorities drastically increased the legal monthly wages of state enterprise workers, office staff, and civil servants by at least 10 to over 20 times, most North Korean residents welcomed it. Expectations were high that they could eat three meals a day and enjoy basic living, but in just 3 to 4 years, massive inflation caused by shortages, and currency devaluation hit the public economy hard.
RFA sources reported that most workers do not expect wages to serve as a means of livelihood, pointing out the severe gap between state-fixed wages and individual day labor. They criticized North Korea as “socialist in appearance, but more capitalist than actual capitalism.”
Winter brings high coal costs
In November, an even bigger crisis is facing the Kim household: heat. Coal prices have skyrocketed to 800,000–900,000 won per metric ton, more than quadruple the cost just six years ago.
In North Korea, a four-member household usually needs at minimum 1 to 1.5 metric tons of coal to get through winter. To actually be warm, they need at least 3 metric tons, but the Kims decided to stick to minimal heating. Preparing firewood for the winter should have started back in the summer, but Mr. Kim, burdened with monthly budget deficits and struggling just to put food on the table, had no time to spare.
North Korea's Kaephung county is seen from the observatory of the Aegibong Peace Ecopark in Gimpo, South Korea, Nov. 29, 2024.
(Lee Jin-man/AP) Families must also prepare food supplies to get them through the winter, and this has traditionally been done through kimjang, where families gather together and make large amounts of kimchi – enough to last through the colder half of the year.
Sources told RFA that the vegetables that go into kimchi are expensive: napa cabbage currently costs 9,000 to 10,000 won per kilogram, while radishes cost 7,000 to 8,000 won per kilogram. While a family of four typically needs around 300 kilograms of cabbage for the season, the Kim household plans to prepare a minimal batch of 30 kilograms of cabbage kimchi and 10 kilograms of radish kimchi without extra seasonings. Even this reduced batch costs at least 340,000 won, driving the family deeper into debt.
Sources estimate that a four-person household in North Korea needs approximately $80 to $100 USD (roughly 5.9 million to 7.8 million North Korean won) per month for baseline survival, yet ordinary residents operate on less than half that amount. Even if Ms. Lee works day labor and side jobs all month to earn 3 million won, the family still reaches only half of the required subsistence threshold.
RFA asked Ishimaru how ordinary North Korean families manage to survive under persistent deficits.
“I’m really curious too. Truly curious,” Ishimaru said. “Residents in provincial cities live under very difficult conditions. Everyone assesses that life was much more comfortable before 2019, … when individual economic activities were possible.”
To make matters worse, sources project that as usual, grain prices will rise again starting in December as the worst months of winter roll in. Mr. Kim will continue working at the factory to receive 20,000 won. To cover the deficit budget of their 4-member family, his wife Ms. Lee will have to find unofficial work at 100,000 won a day for at least half the month of December to make ends meet, even on their family’s tightened budget.
Edited by Noh Jung Min in Korean and by Charlie Dharapak and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: No internet, no advance warning: 11 killed in Myanmar military bombing in Sagaing
articles.excerpt: Civilians in war zones are left vulnerable as Starlink internet becomes scarce after scam center crackdown.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
It was just before noon on Saturday. Three gyrocopters flew low as they approached Nyaung Pin Lay village. A school and surrounding residential area was bombed. Eleven were killed, including four children.
A resident told RFA that although the local People’s Defense Forces (PDF) received a tip that the Myanmar military would bomb the school, the warning could not reach them in time due to the lack of internet in the village.
“Information that this would be bombed was sent online to everyone. They did inform us,” the Kani Township resident told RFA on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“But because there was no Starlink communication, casualties were high as a result. About a month ago in Nat La Po village, when we got the exact location that would be bombed and cleared the area, there were no casualties. That was fortunate. But now, even though we got the location to be bombed, communication was cut off.”
A May 25, 2025, photo shows a Starlink sign at an internet cafe in Demoso, Myanmar.
(AFP) In Myanmar, home to the world’s longest-running civil war, the military-appointed government has cut off phone lines and internet communications in over 40 percent of townships nationwide. Locals, civil society groups, and revolutionary forces tell RFA that they rely on Starlink — acquiring the devices through unofficial and often expensive channels — as a lifeline for information.
In October 2025, SpaceX announced the disabling of over 2,500 Starlink kits in Myanmar to crack down on transnational cyber-scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border. Subsequent restrictions by SpaceX on unregistered units bought outside of Myanmar have shut down countless others.
Since June, more than 20 percent of Starlink internet devices used in Myanmar have had their services cut off, according to a report released on Oct. 23 by the group Athan.
Local residents and human rights activists told RFA that this has created a crisis for the survival of civilians in areas of intense civil conflict.
A Myanmar government photo taken on Oct. 20, 2025, shows seized Starlink devices during a raid on the KK Park online scam center in Myawaddy.
(Myanmar Military Information Team via AFP) “The military cutting off phone lines and internet connections from the start was intentionally aimed at concealing human rights violations they commit and restricting people’s freedom of expression,” said Joy, a research director at Athan, a non-profit organization for the Freedom of Expression Movement in Myanmar.
“If Starlink also stops providing services to Myanmar and cuts connections, emergency humanitarian aid, air strike alerts, news regarding military columns, and natural disaster warnings for these local residents will stop immediately.”
According to a report titled “Dead Air” released by Athan on October 23, the communication cut-off directly affects the lives and safety of people in conflict-affected regions as they can no longer receive warnings about airstrikes and military movements, medical aid, or updates on family members’ safety and evacuation routes.
RFA contacted Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military-appointed president’s office, regarding when internet and phone lines might be restored. She instead referred RFA to the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications.
Now, not only Starlink devices used by scam operations are being shut down, but Starlink connections used by civilians have also been suspended starting in June this year, with more than 20 percent of devices cut off by October, according to Athan. Consequently, regions like Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, Rakhine, Kayah State, and other areas experiencing severe conflict were directly affected, Athan’s report states.
RFA contacted SpaceX regarding the impact on civilians in regions where the internet has been cut off, but has not received a response at the time of publication.
“Some of our Starlink devices were disabled. This has caused a lot of trouble for us,” said Aye Myint Aung Aung, Head of the Department of Humanitarian Assistance and Emergency Management under the Mandalay Regional Interim Administrative Council.
“On the other hand, whether it’s our civilians, revolutionary groups, or those leading and operating the administrative mechanism in revolutionary forces, everyone relies on Starlink. As access to information becomes more restricted, limitations on civilian safety also increase. I would define this as a very major challenge for us.”
In Kayah State, Deputy Minister of Defense for the Karenni State Government Khu Daniel told RFA that Starlink connections are being shut down one by one, raising concerns.
“For the public and for the youth currently fighting in battle, it will become a cause for concern,” he said.
A Sept. 17, 2025, photo shows people on a balcony of a building with what appears to be Starlink satellite dishes on the roof in the KK Park complex in Myawaddy, Myanmar.
(Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP) Khun Chit Htoo, who is assisting refugees in the Karenni Region, said that if all Starlink services are shut down, it could have a severe impact on humanitarian aid operations.
“Our current work relies on internet connectivity as well as donors. Since we connect online, we are very concerned,” said Khun Chit Htoo.
“We will face a situation where we can no longer help needy civilians receive the support they really need across all aspects of coordination. If there is no internet line left, I believe we stand to lose a lot because of this single connection.”
While welcoming and supporting the shutdown of Starlink internet lines used by online scam operations to crack down on scam syndicates, 317 civil society organizations issued a statement on July 17 expressing deep concern over potential negative impacts if all Starlink terminals nationwide are shut down.
According to an October 23 report by the Myanmar Internet Project, an organization monitoring internet shutdowns and conflicts, there were 581 military airstrikes that killed at least 353 civilians in the three months from July to September 2026, with 562 of those attacks occurring in areas where internet service was cut off.
Translated by Nayrein Kyaw. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: A trip to the South Korean seaside for glimpses of my North Korean hometown
articles.excerpt: Escapee Park Sol-ji often gets homesick for the port city of Chongjin. A beach day in Busan comes close.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Park Sol-ji stared out over the water at Gwangalli Beach with the iconic Gwangan Bridge in the distance, just above the horizon. South Korea’s touristy second largest city of Busan is a drastic change from heavily industrialized Chongjin – her hometown in North Korea. But both cities are large ports on the eastern side of the peninsula, and the sand, the breeze, and the smell of the sea reminds her of home.
“I love looking at the sea, and coming here whenever I miss my hometown is a big part of it,” she told Radio Free Asia Nov. 3. “Also, coming to the seaside makes me feel like I can finally breathe. I think I like it because it gives me such a sense of liberation.”
Park Sol-ji is a pseudonym she is using for safety reasons. Sol-ji fled North Korea 19 years ago when she was 20 years old, arriving in South Korea the following year. Adjusting to life in the fast-paced South was jarring. Though she tried her best to blend in among South Korean 20-somethings , it would all come crashing down whenever she spoke with her unmistakable North Korean accent.
She often found the degree of change in her life to be overwhelming, and she longed to return home, but that was now impossible. In times like that a trip to the sea would always remind her just enough of home to boost her spirits.
These days, she’s shed the accent and looks about the same as everyone else, but she still gets homesick and often travels to the seaside.
A map showing the locations of Chongjin, North Korea and Busan, South Korea.
(RFA) Busan is very different from Chongjin. Though both cities are industrialized ports, the South Korean city has – over many decades – invested in travel infrastructure and branded itself as a global tourist destination.
According to tourism statistics compiled by the Busan city government, more than 3.93 million foreign tourists have already visited Busan this year alone. CNN introduced Busan as “Asia’s Next Coastal City,” and Expedia selected Busan as the only Korean destination among its “Top 10 Destinations of the Year for 2027.”
But for Sol-ji, it’s not the glitz and glamor she’s coming for. She is here to take in the memories of the seaside of her childhood, where she played in the sand with her friends and spent precious moments with her family.
Memories roll in with the rising tide
Though the forecast called for cloudy weather, Gwangalli Beach had quite a few visitors from midday, perhaps due to the unexpectedly clear sky. Couples were taking photos with the sea as a backdrop, groups of noisy students on a field trip made their way across the sand, and foreign tourists walked barefoot. Everyone had smiles on their faces. Gwangalli Beach is well known as a romantic spot where the blue sea harmonizes with the spectacular night view of the Gwangan Bridge.
Sol-ji slowly surveyed the seascape and her face lit up as she spoke of the days she and her family would break out a large cauldron, build a fire, catch fish, and cook eojuk, a type of spicy fish porridge. She also remembered how she and her friends used to play by pulling up seaweed to gather in makeshift nets made of their extra clothes. Although these were ordinary childhood games, looking back now, they were moments she can never have again. To her, the sea is a landscape she longs for, as well as a place where she finds solace for her wounds.
“I even dreamt of returning to Chongjin because I missed my hometown, but even in the dream, seeing my dyed hair and decorated nails, I thought I would get caught,” she said. North Korea is notorious for fashion police who crack down on “capitalist” looks like dyed hair, colored nails, blue jeans, clothing with English words and phrases, and other no-nos. In South Korea, Sol-ji is free to dress how she wants to, but that does not erase her longing.
“I really do want to go back just once.”
The old village in the hills
Prior to visiting the beach, Sol-ji had started the day with a train ride to Busan Station, disembarking in the morning. The first spot on her itinerary was Gamcheon Culture Village, a 10-minute taxi ride away. The village started as a ramshackle town built up in the hills for laborers, and it expanded greatly with the swell of refugees fleeing to Busan from the advancing North Korean army in the opening weeks of the 1950-53 Korean War. In recent years the village was painstakingly restored through cultural preservation and beautification projects.
These days, tourists flock to its narrow meandering streets, attracted by the colorfully painted houses, many of which have been converted to shops, cafes and mini-museums. Near the high point of the village sits a colorful statue of the Little Prince, presiding over a space dedicated to the mythos presented in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s world-renowned novella.
A statue of the Little Prince and the fox at the Little Prince House in Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea.
(Saha-gu Office via korea.net) Today, the tourists have come in force. More often than not, passersby who came for the village’s unique artsy flair will be speaking in a language other than Korean.
While most tourists are browsing the shops, ordering refreshments, or taking in one of the museums, Sol-ji slowly looks around the alley, finally focusing on a clothesline in the courtyard of one house. She noticed three or four items of clothing hanging on a single line, swaying in the breeze. It was this evidence that people actually live here that conjured up the feelings of her childhood.
“People here hang their laundry on clotheslines like that. It’s exactly the same in North Korea,” she said. She explained that in North Korea some families have washing machines, but rolling blackouts are common in most places, so people still have to do laundry by hand.
“So here they also dry their laundry in the sun,” she said. “Knowing this is quite heartwarming.”
In another area of town she operated a manual pump that once drew water out of the ground. She said it made her think of her grandmother’s house in Chongjin.
Sol-ji walked along, looking around every corner of the alley. Though sun-dried laundry and the hand pump might be similar details, the nature of this town, built up on a hillside, would never make sense in Chongjin, she said.
Park Sol-ji, visits Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “There aren’t many houses on slopes like this in Chongjin. It costs a lot of money to build roads and houses up to these inclines,” she said. “Instead, there are many fields on these mountain slopes. It is land where people make a living through farming.”
Noon approached, and it was time for lunch.
Food for reminiscing
Sol-ji’s next destination was the famous open-air Jagalchi seafood market. As she walked from stall to stall, the boisterous calls of merchants mingled together, as they tried to attract customers by shouting out prices in their folksy Busan accents while holding up wriggling fish. Jagalchi is the largest seafood market in the country, and it is another big Busan tourist destination.
Sol-ji looked around the market, carefully observing the fish leaping out of the ice. She seemed to be searching for familiar fish such as flounder, cutlassfish, mackerel, and squid. Although it was an unfamiliar market, the seafood displayed on the stalls was something she often saw back in her hometown, she said.
She recalled how North and South Koreans use different words for squid and two types of octopus and this led to confusion.
문어 (muneo) 낙지 (nakji) 오징어 (ojingeo)
North Korea all octopus varieties squid cuttlefish
South Korea large octopus varieties small octopus varieties squid and cuttlefish
“We called squid nakji . So when I’m here and I see the small octopus that they’re calling nakji , that’s what we used to call baby muneo ,” said Sol-ji.
She recalled that during her childhood she would often snack on dried squid, tearing off tasty parts and chewing it by the mouthful.
The marketplace also conjured up memories of eating raw fish, but the way she enjoyed it up North was very different. In Chongjin raw fish is served slathered in a thick sauce, and wrapped with other ingredients in lettuce. But she was surprised when she came to South Korea and saw people eat the plain white flesh dipped in only a little bit of sauce.
Park Sol-ji visits Jagalchi seafood market in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “I think the seafood I ate in Chongjin was tastier,” she said, smiling broadly. She explained that fish caught in colder places is saltier and tastier.
But then again, she said, it might have just been that she was hungry all the time back then.
“It’s like something out of a dream.”
As the sun set behind Gwangalli Beach, Gwangan Bridge lit up the night sky in a dazzling flash of color. Sol-ji got in line to ride a yacht under the bridge, out to sea to catch the fireworks show exclusively for the passengers.
Park Sol-ji views the city of Busan, South Korea at night off Gwangalli Beach, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) As the yacht moved along, Sol-ji couldn’t help but notice that it was a stark difference from the pitch black nighttime seascape in Chongjin – out at sea, Busan’s night sky is brightly and colorfully illuminated by the bridge, the cityscape – and soon, the fireworks.
Sol-ji sat on the deck, quietly closing her eyes and feeling the sea breeze. Then in one magic moment, lights shot out of the sky with a loud boom. The fireworks brought a bright smile across her face.
In all her excitement, her thoughts drifted to her childhood friends. Although they live in different places now, she thought how wonderful it would be if they could gaze at the dazzling night sea of ​​Busan together.
A yacht tour fireworks display in the waters off Gwangalli Beach in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “This really feels like a dream, but I really do want to try it with them at least once,” she said. “I want to take lots of photos with my friends and go sightseeing like this.”
Under the glowing bursts, she reflected on her current daily life. Nothing like this would ever be possible in North Korea, she said. But in South Korea she can go wherever she wants, with whomever she wants, wearing whatever she wants. She smiled, realizing that “freedom” isn’t a grandiose ideal or political buzzword, it is contained in an ordinary moment like this, on a boat at sea near Busan, under the brightly lit night sky.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: North Korean orphans fast tracked into state care to stem declining birth rate
articles.excerpt: Orphanages are now supplied more regularly after shift toward birth-friendly policies.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
North Korea is attempting to address its decreasing birth rate by improving the conditions of state-run orphanages while increasing crackdowns on illegal abortions, residents in the country told Radio Free Asia.
The total fertility rate for North Korea is estimated to be 1.59 children per woman of childbearing age according to key statistical indicators from South Korea’s Ministry of Data and Statistics. This is well below the replacement fertility rate of 2.1 required to maintain the population.
The rate may be even lower than estimated, a 2025 report by the Washington-based Stimson Center’s 38 North project said.
Orphanages and nurseries were previously poorly supplied, meaning that taking in more children was difficult, but government policies have improved the situation, with supplies of milk, food, clothing and shoes flowing in more regularly, the residents said.
School children arrive to pay their respects before the statues of late North Korean leaders Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il at Mansu Hill in Pyongyang on Sept. 9, 2023.
(Kim Won Jin/AFP) “Recently, authorities have been more quickly sending orphaned children or children born to unmarried women to nurseries or orphanages,” a resident of the country’s northeastern province of North Hamgyong, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told RFA. “The residents’ reaction to this is generally positive.”
The resident talked about a situation where an unmarried woman from Kyongwon county, on the border with China, had to give up her child because of the difficulty raising it alone. The child was quickly accepted into an orphanage in October.
Though the resident did not specify how long it took to place the child, another resident, from nearby South Hamgyong province, told RFA that in another case, in the coastal city of Tanchon, it took about a month.
“In September, in Tanchon, a 6-year-old child became an orphan after his mother, who had been raising him alone, died of illness,” the South Hamgyong resident said on condition of anonymity to speak freely. The child “went to an orphanage after about a month.”
Supplies meeting demand
The government’s apparent priority on supplying nurseries and orphanages has come after a series of child-friendly policies were enacted including the Childcare Law of 2022 and the Law on Preferential Treatment for Multi-Child Families of 2025. Authorities actively encourage childbirth and child-rearing, including by pushing propaganda messaging that “having many babies is patriotism.”
A woman receives the "Communist Mother's Honor Award" during the Fifth National Mothers' Convention in Pyongyang, North Korea, Dec. 4, 2023.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) The country’s leader Kim Jong Un famously was brought to tears in 2023 when he publicly discussed the declining birth rate at the National Mothers’ Conference in December 2023.
“Putting our efforts into raising the birth rate together with mothers is a critical revolutionary undertaking that cannot be resolved by the power of our Party and government alone,” he said at the event.
Sources in RFA reports after that incident explained that women were reluctant to marry and have kids because they wanted to focus on their own happiness.
Abortion crackdown
Another way the government has been trying to prevent a declining birth rate is to punish doctors who perform abortions .
By law, abortion is illegal in North Korea, but in practice, some doctors accept payment to perform the procedure in secret.
But these days, those doctors are harder to find, the North Hamgyong resident said.
“There are women who come home pregnant after serving in the military, and they try to get rid of the baby quickly before it is seen by others,” the North Hamgyong resident said. “But recently, abortion procedures have not been easy, so many end up giving birth.”
Unwanted pregnancies happen often in North Korea because sex education is non-existent, the North Hamgyong resident said. But even if the mother gives birth, administrative hurdles and societal pressure make it very difficult to raise the child. This is because it is impossible to register the child without the father, and because of the stigma surrounding unwed mothers.
Many unwed mothers are finding creative ways to put their children born out of wedlock in orphanages without having any official record of the birth, the South Hamgyong resident said. “In late September in Tanchon, a resident found a baby wrapped in a sling in a neighborhood alley and took it to the community center.”
Students attend class in North Korea, April 2, 2018.
(KCNA via Reuters) However, it was later revealed that the person who took the child to the community center was actually the maternal uncle of the woman who had given birth, the South Hamgyong resident said. Since the fact that the unmarried woman had given birth might become a major obstacle to marriage if known to the outside world, the uncle had resorted to a workaround for his niece.
The South Hamgyong resident said that the woman did not intend to become pregnant, and had tried to get an abortion but she could not find any doctor willing to provide one.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: International community condemns Joshua Wong’s 10-year ‘foreign collusion’ sentence
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong democracy activist has been in prison since age 23 and is expected to be released around 2036 at…
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Mandarin
After a Hong Kong court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison Thursday for foreign collusion, international lawmakers, activists, and rights organizations condemned the decision saying it violates human rights.
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong gets 10 more years under security law
Wong, 30, is one of the most internationally recognizable faces of the now-quashed democracy movement in the city. He was among 45 Hong Kong opposition politicians and pro-democracy activists who were convicted of “conspiracy to commit subversion” under the city’s draconian 2020 National Security Law for taking part in a democratic primary in the summer of 2020. Wong in September pleaded guilty to “conspiracy to endanger national security with foreign or external forces.”
